task_row_model.query: A 62-year-old man with recently diagnosed small-cell lung cancer on immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy develops two weeks of subacute memory loss, behavioral change and a focal seizure. How can I distinguish paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis from herpes simplex virus (HSV) encephalitis, which initial diagnostic tests should I order urgently, and what empiric treatments are recommended while awaiting results?

documents.content: HSV encephalitis diagnosis relies on rapid cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) testing and neuroimaging. CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated protein; HSV PCR on CSF has high sensitivity and specificity but can be falsely negative in the very early hours of illness. Brain MRI commonly shows T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in the medial temporal lobes and insula, often asymmetric and necrotizing. EEG may show periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges. Because untreated HSV can be rapidly destructive, empiric high‑dose intravenous acyclovir should be started immediately when HSV is a diagnostic possibility, and continued until PCR reliably excludes infection.

Cognitive impairment after systemic chemotherapy is a recognized syndrome termed 'chemo brain' characterized by attention deficits, slowed processing, and memory complaints that may persist for months. Neuroimaging is usually non-specific; formal neuropsychological testing can quantify domains affected. Management focuses on cognitive rehabilitation, addressed comorbidities (sleep, mood), and occupational strategies. This disorder is typically insidious, non-febrile, and not associated with focal seizures, CSF pleocytosis, or focal medial temporal lobe signal changes on MRI, distinguishing it from inflammatory or infectious encephalitides.

Distinguishing paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis (PLE) from HSV encephalitis requires integrating clinical course, MRI, CSF studies, and targeted testing. Both can produce subacute memory loss and medial temporal FLAIR hyperintensity. Key differences: HSV often has acute febrile presentation, more necrotic and asymmetric MRI changes, and characteristic EEG patterns; CSF HSV PCR is diagnostic when positive. PLE is associated with onconeural antibodies (eg, anti‑Hu with small‑cell lung cancer) and may present more insidiously. Urgent tests: brain MRI with contrast, EEG, CSF cell count/protein, CSF HSV PCR, and CSF/serum paraneoplastic autoantibody panel. Initial management: start empiric IV acyclovir promptly to cover HSV; if infectious studies are negative and PLE is likely, begin immunotherapy (high‑dose IV methylprednisolone, IVIG or plasmapheresis) while coordinating oncologic treatment.

Paraneoplastic antibody testing (serum and CSF) can identify specific syndromes; anti‑Hu (ANNA‑1) is classically linked to small‑cell lung cancer and limbic dysfunction. However, antibody panels are not uniformly sensitive: clinical suspicion and compatible imaging can warrant empiric immunotherapy even with negative antibodies. First‑line immune treatments include high‑dose intravenous corticosteroids, IVIG, and plasma exchange; early tumor control is also critical since removal or treatment of the underlying malignancy may improve neurologic outcome. Close monitoring for steroid effects and infection is required, particularly in patients on immunotherapy for cancer.

Seizures in patients with brain metastases are treated acutely with benzodiazepines and antiepileptic drugs; prophylactic anticonvulsants are not recommended for patients with brain metastases who have not had a seizure. When indicated, levetiracetam is often preferred due to minimal drug–drug interactions with chemotherapy and targeted agents. Phenytoin and carbamazepine have substantial interactions and are less favored. Management also includes addressing intracranial mass effect with steroids and considering surgical resection or stereotactic radiosurgery for accessible lesions causing seizures.
